entry: Men's association football team representing Italy, governed by the Italian Football Federation (FIGC). Its first official match was played in Milan on May 15, 1910. Nicknamed *gli Azzurri* (the Blues), Italy has won the [[FIFA World Cup]] four times (1934, 1938, 1982, and 2006), becoming the first team to successfully defend the title, and it has won the [[UEFA European Championship]] twice (1968 and 2020). Italy failed to qualify for the 2018 and 2022 World Cups. Its training center is in [[Florence]].

Emperor (tsar) of Bulgaria (r. 1218–1241). He was the son of Ivan Asen I, a founder of the [[Second Bulgarian Empire]], who was killed in 1196. After Kaloyan was murdered in 1207, Boril, another nephew of Kaloyan, was proclaimed emperor, and Ivan Asen fled to the Rus' principalities. He returned to Bulgaria, captured Tarnovo, and blinded Boril in 1218. At the Battle of Klokotnitsa in 1230 he defeated Theodore Komnenos Doukas of the Empire of Thessalonica and conquered large territories in Macedonia, Thessaly, and Thrace. In 1235 he concluded an alliance with the Empire of Nicaea, and at the same meeting the head of the Bulgarian Church was granted the rank of patriarch, in token of its autocephaly. He broke off the alliance in 1237. He also struck gold coins at a new mint in Ohrid.

Russian writer and first Russian Nobel laureate in Literature (1933). Born on his parental estate in Voronezh, Bunin carried on the classical traditions of [[Russian literature]] in prose and [[Poetry|poetry]]. His best-known works include the short novels *The Village* (1910) and *Dry Valley* (1912), the autobiographical novel *The Life of Arseniev*, and the short story collection *Dark Avenues* (1946). He also published the diary *Cursed Days* (1926), covering 1917–1918. He left Russia after the Bolshevik Revolution and settled mainly in France. Bunin was revered by Russian émigrés and many fellow writers, who viewed him as an heir to the tradition of realism established by Tolstoy and Chekhov.

Grand Prince of [[Moscow]] and all Russia (r. 1462–1505), also known as Ivan the Great. He served as co-ruler and regent for his blind father, Vasily II, before taking the throne. Ivan multiplied the territory of his state through conquest, purchase, inheritance, and seizure of dynastic lands, and laid the foundations of a centralized Russian state. He renovated the [[Kremlin]] and introduced a new legal code. He ended [[Tatars|Tatar]] dominance over Russia; his victory over the Great Horde in 1480 formally restored its independence. Ivan began using the title tsar in his correspondence with other monarchs, but at home he was satisfied with the title of grand prince. Through his marriage to Sophia Palaiologina, he made the double-headed eagle Russia's coat of arms and adopted the idea of Moscow as the third Rome. His 43-year reign was the second-longest in Russian history, after that of his grandson Ivan IV.

Russian and Soviet experimental physiologist. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904 for research on the physiology of digestion, and he is known for discovering classical conditioning through experiments with dogs. Pavlov attended the Ryazan church school and theological seminary before abandoning a religious career. In 1870 he enrolled at the University of [[Saint Petersburg]] to study natural science. He investigated the circulatory system for his medical dissertation. His later experiments identified [[Reflex|conditioned reflexes]]: a neutral stimulus, repeatedly paired with food, came to produce salivation on its own. He mentored a prolific school of researchers in higher nervous activity.

Russian novelist, short-story writer, and playwright. Born in Oryol to noble parents, he studied philosophy and history at the University of Berlin and became a popularizer of [[Russian literature]] in the West. He began a civil service career in 1841, but like many educated contemporaries he was opposed to serfdom. His first major publication, the short story collection *A Sportsman's Sketches* (1852), was a milestone of Russian realism. His novel *Fathers and Sons* (1862) is regarded as one of the major works of 19th-century fiction. He spent much of his later life in Western Europe, mainly in Baden-Baden or [[Paris]]. He never married.

First tsar of all Russia (r. 1547–1584). He succeeded his father as grand prince of [[Moscow]] in 1533, at the age of three, and was crowned tsar in 1547. He established the Zemsky Sobor, a new assembly, revised the legal code, and created the first Russian standing army, the streltsy. He conquered the khanates of [[Kazan]] and Astrakhan, bringing the entire length of the [[Volga]] under Russian control. He triggered the [[Livonian War]] (1558–1583), which ravaged Russia, failed to take Livonia, and cost it Ingria. He conducted a violent purge through the oprichniki, Russia's first political police. In the later years of his reign, the oprichniki massacred Novgorod and [[Tatars|Crimean Tatars]] burned Moscow. Historians generally believe that in a fit of anger he murdered his eldest son and heir, Ivan Ivanovich. The epithet *grozny* is usually translated as terrible, though modern scholars suggest formidable or awe-inspiring.

Antiparasitic medication of the avermectin family. Discovered in 1975, it was first used in veterinary medicine and approved for human use in 1987. It treats head lice, [[Scabies|scabies]], river blindness (onchocerciasis), and lymphatic filariasis. It interferes with the nerves and muscles of parasites, leading to paralysis. William Campbell and Satoshi Ōmura were awarded the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for its discovery and applications. Claims that it treats [[COVID-19]] lack credible scientific support; major health organizations advise against its use for that disease.

Hard, white material from the tusks and teeth of animals, consisting mainly of dentin. The chemical structure of mammalian teeth and tusks is the same regardless of species, so the term ivory can describe any mammalian teeth or tusks of commercial interest that are large enough to carve. Elephant ivory is the most important source, but ivory from [[Mammoth|mammoth]], [[Walrus|walrus]], hippopotamus, [[Sperm whale|sperm whale]], [[Narwhal|narwhal]], and warthog is also used. Ivory has been valued since ancient times for carvings, false teeth, piano keys, fans, and [[Dominoes|dominoes]]. Trade in finished ivory products has its origins in the Indus Valley, where pins, combs, and dice were found at Harappan sites. In Japan, ivory carvings became popular in the 17th century during the [[Edo period]]. Trade in natural ivory of threatened species, such as African and Asian elephants, is illegal.

Country on the southern coast of West Africa, officially the Republic of Côte d'Ivoire. Its capital is Yamoussoukro, while its largest city and economic center is the port city of [[Abidjan]]. It borders Guinea, Liberia, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Ghana. French is the official language. The area became a French protectorate in 1843 and a colony in 1893 amid the [[Scramble for Africa]]. It achieved independence in 1960 under [[Félix Houphouët-Boigny]], who ruled until 1993. Its stability was diminished by a *coup d'état* in 1999 and civil wars from 2002 to 2007 and again in 2010–2011. From 2012 to 2023 the economy grew by an average of 7.1% per year in real terms. As of 2023, it is the world's largest exporter of [[Cocoa bean|cocoa beans]]. As of the most recent survey, in 2016, 46.1% of the population remained affected by multidimensional poverty.

Athletic conference of eight private research universities in the Northeastern United States. Its members are Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, Pennsylvania, Princeton, and Yale. The name is also used for these schools, which are associated with academic excellence and highly selective admissions. The league competes in [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] Division I, and its name became official in 1954. All members except Cornell were founded in the colonial period. All eight belong to the Association of American Universities.

Japanese entertainer and shrine maiden (*miko*) traditionally credited with creating [[Kabuki|kabuki]] theater. She served as a *miko* at the Izumo Grand Shrine before being sent to [[Kyoto]] to perform sacred dances. Her adaptation of the *nembutsu* dance, a largely secular folk dance, was known for its sultriness and sexual innuendo. From around 1603 she performed on the dry riverbed of the Kamo River, and her all-female troupe quickly gained popularity. The troupe was exclusively female, so Okuni required her actresses to play both male and female roles. Many imitators, particularly brothels, followed her style, and in 1629 a ban on women performers shifted kabuki to male-only troupes. Few details of her life are known; she retired and disappeared around 1610.

Method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly those produced by [[Digital photography|digital photography]]. It typically achieves 10:1 compression with a perceptible but widely accepted loss of quality. The Joint Photographic Experts Group created the standard in 1992, based on the discrete cosine transform. JPEG has been the most widely used image compression standard in the world, with several billion JPEG images produced every day as of 2015. In 2000 the JPEG group introduced JPEG 2000 as a successor, but it did not replace the original as the dominant standard.

American multinational banking institution headquartered in New York City. It is the largest bank in the United States and is considered systemically important by the Financial Stability Board. The firm was created in 2000 by the merger of J.P. Morgan & Co. and Chase Manhattan Company. Its oldest predecessor, the Bank of the Manhattan Company, was founded in 1799 by [[Aaron Burr]]. It operates the largest investment bank in the world by revenue. Critics point to its risk management, its broad financing activities, and its large-scale legal settlements.

American writer best known for the novel *The Catcher in the Rye* (1951). Its depiction of adolescent alienation was influential. He published stories in *Story* magazine in 1940 and served in [[World War II]]. Its success brought public attention, and Salinger became reclusive, publishing less often. His later works include *Nine Stories* (1953) and *Franny and Zooey* (1961). His last published work, the novella *Hapworth 16, 1924*, appeared in 1965. He died of natural causes.

American law enforcement administrator and first director of the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]]. President [[Calvin Coolidge]] appointed him director of the Bureau of Investigation in 1924, and he led both agencies for 48 years under eight presidents. He expanded the FBI and introduced a centralized [[Fingerprint|fingerprint]] file and forensic laboratories. Later investigations found that he routinely violated FBI policies and laws, used the bureau to harass political dissidents and civil rights leaders, and collected information through illegal surveillance and burglaries.

British physicist, discoverer of the electron. In 1897 he showed that cathode rays consisted of negatively charged particles, now called [[Electron|electrons]], much smaller than atoms and with a very large charge-to-mass ratio. The electron was the first subatomic particle discovered. In 1912 he found the first evidence for [[Isotope|isotopes]] of a stable element, and with Francis William Aston he made the first use of [[Mass spectrometry|mass spectrometry]]. He became Cavendish Professor of Physics at [[Cambridge]] in 1884 and received the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics for investigations into the conduction of electricity by gases. Seven of his students won Nobel Prizes, including [[Ernest Rutherford]]. His son, George Paget Thomson, shared the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physics for the diffraction of electrons by crystals.

British author of the fantasy series *Harry Potter*. Its seven volumes have sold over 600 million copies, making it the best-selling book series in history. Rowling conceived the series in 1990, and the first novel, *Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone*, was published in 1997. She also writes the crime series *Cormoran Strike* under the name Robert Galbraith. In 2008 Forbes named her the world's highest-paid author. From 2019 she has made public remarks on transgender issues, including opposition to gender self-identification, that have drawn criticism.

American actor and voice performer, known for character roles on film and television. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance as an abusive jazz instructor in *Whiplash* (2014). He played J. Jonah Jameson in Sam Raimi's *Spider-Man* trilogy and reprised the role in Marvel films. On television he played a white supremacist prisoner in *Oz* and Dr. Emil Skoda in *Law & Order*. His voice roles include Cave Johnson in *Portal 2* and Omni-Man in *Invincible*.

South African and Australian novelist, essayist, and translator. Born in [[Cape Town]], he studied mathematics and English at the University of Cape Town, graduating with honors in both subjects. He taught English literature at the State University of New York at Buffalo and was on the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]]'s Committee on Social Thought until 2003. He won the 2003 Nobel Prize in Literature and has won the [[Booker Prize]] twice. He moved to Australia in 2002, became an Australian citizen in 2006, and lives in [[Adelaide]]. His fictionalized memoirs *Boyhood* (1997) and *Youth* (2002) recount his early life. His most recent book is *The Pole and Other Stories* (2023).

English Romantic painter, celebrated for landscapes and renditions of light and atmosphere. Known during his lifetime as William Turner, he began as an architectural draughtsman and watercolorist before gaining recognition as an oil painter. He entered the Royal Academy of Arts at 14 and became a Royal Academician in his twenties. His use of light and atmosphere inspired the early [[Impressionism|impressionist]] painters [[Claude Monet]] and [[Camille Pissarro]]. Some critics in aristocratic circles repeatedly criticized him for his working-class origins. His later, more abstract landscapes were poorly received at the time but are now considered masterpieces. He kept several second homes on or near the [[River Thames|Thames]]. He died wealthy, and his most important works are displayed at the [[National Gallery]] and Tate Britain in London.

American financier and investment banker who dominated corporate finance on [[Wall Street]] during the [[Gilded Age]] and the Progressive Era. He headed the banking firm that became [[JPMorgan Chase]]. He spearheaded the formation of U.S. Steel, International Harvester, and [[General Electric]], and he and his partners held controlling interests in Aetna, Western Union, the Pullman Car Company, and 21 railroads. During the Panic of 1907 he organized a coalition of financiers to address the crisis. Adrian Wooldridge characterized him as America's greatest banker. Biographer Ron Chernow estimated his fortune at $80 million. He died in [[Rome]], leaving his fortune and business to his son, J. P. Morgan Jr.

English writer and philologist, author of the high fantasy works *The Hobbit* and *The Lord of the Rings*. He was Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at the [[University of Oxford]] from 1925 to 1945, then Merton Professor of English Language and Literature until 1959. A devout Catholic, he was a close friend of [[C. S. Lewis]] and a member of the Inklings. In 1972 [[Elizabeth II]] appointed him a Commander of the Order of the British Empire. After his death, his son Christopher published works from his notes, including *The Silmarillion*. Together with his novels, these works form a connected body of tales set in Middle-earth. He is popularly identified as the father of modern fantasy literature.

American theoretical physicist, often called the father of the atomic bomb. He directed the [[Manhattan Project]]'s Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II and witnessed the first atomic bomb test, [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity]], on July 16, 1945. The atomic bombings of [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|Hiroshima and Nagasaki]] followed in August. He made major contributions to quantum mechanics, [[Quantum electrodynamics|quantum electrodynamics]], and to astrophysics, including the theory of neutron stars and [[Black hole|black holes]]. After the war he directed the Institute for Advanced Study and opposed development of the hydrogen bomb, partly on ethical grounds. In 1954 an Atomic Energy Commission security hearing led to the revocation of his security clearance; the decision was vacated in 2022.

Prehistoric period of [[Japan]], named for [[Pottery|pottery]] decorated with cord impressions. It lasted from c. 14,000 to 300 BC and was inhabited by the Jōmon people, diverse [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]] and early agriculturalists with a common culture. Their ancestors migrated from Northeast Asia, the Korean Peninsula, [[China]], and [[Southeast Asia]]. The period is conventionally divided into six phases: Incipient, Initial, Early, Middle, Late, and Final. It is rich in tools and jewelry of bone, stone, shell, and antler, as well as pottery figurines, vessels, and lacquerware. The Jōmon people eventually admixed with the Yayoi people, whose period began between 500 and 300 BC according to [[Radiocarbon dating|radiocarbon]] evidence. Modern Japanese carry approximately 30% paternal ancestry from the Jōmon.
